raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure due to left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, when no alternative cause is evident [1,2]. Contemporary definitions usually require an LV ejection fraction (LVEF) <45%, with or without LV dilatation, and emphasize that PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion [3-6]. Although initially described as a rare disorder, population studies show marked geographic and ethnic variation, from approximately 1 in 1000–4000 births in many Western cohorts to substantially higher rates in parts of Africa and Haiti [7-12].

Risk factors include African ancestry, advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and possibly socioeconomic and nutritional factors [7-14]. The epidemiology is clinically important because PPCM remains a major contributor to maternal morbidity, intensive care admission, transplantation, and death. In the United States, incidence appears to have risen over time, partly reflecting older maternal age, improved recognition, and higher prevalence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy [8-11,13].

Pathogenesis is heterogeneous. Early observations suggested inflammation, myocarditis, autoimmunity, and abnormal immune tolerance after pregnancy [15]. A central mechanistic advance was the “prolactin hypothesis”: oxidative stress activates cathepsin D cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa fragment that is antiangiogenic, proapoptotic, and cardiotoxic [16]. A complementary angiogenic model implicates late-pregnancy elevation of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt1), reduced vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, endothelial dysfunction, and myocardial microvascular injury, providing a biologic link with pre-eclampsia and multiple gestation [17]. Genetic susceptibility is also important; truncating variants, particularly in TTN, overlap with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy and may predict incomplete recovery or familial risk [18,19]. PPCM is therefore best regarded as a pregnancy-triggered cardiomyopathy in genetically or biologically susceptible women.

Symptoms often overlap with normal late pregnancy—dyspnea, fatigue, edema, orthopnea—so diagnosis requires vigilance. Red flags include resting tachycardia, hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, elevated jugular venous pressure, new murmur, S3 gallop, syncope, embolic events, or persistent symptoms after delivery. Evaluation includes electrocardiography, natriuretic peptides, chest imaging when indicated, and echocardiography to quantify LVEF, LV size, right ventricular function, pulmonary pressures, valvular disease, and intracardiac thrombus [20-23]. BNP or NT-proBNP is usually elevated in PPCM and is useful because normal pregnancy produces only modest increases. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, preferably postpartum, may help assess ventricular volumes, thrombus, edema, and fibrosis, and exclude alternative cardiomyopathies or myocarditis [24].

Management requires coordinated cardio-obstetric care. During pregnancy, treatment follows heart-failure principles using fetal-compatible agents: loop diuretics for congestion, beta-1 selective beta-blockers, hydralazine plus nitrates for afterload reduction, and digoxin when needed. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are generally avoided until after delivery, although selected postpartum therapies may be compatible with breastfeeding [25,26]. Delivery timing is individualized; hemodynamically stable patients can often continue pregnancy with close surveillance, whereas cardiogenic shock, refractory hypoxemia, malignant arrhythmia, or fetal compromise may require urgent delivery. Vaginal delivery with regional anesthesia is usually preferred unless obstetric indications dictate cesarean section [25].

Because pregnancy and severe LV dysfunction are prothrombotic, anticoagulation is commonly recommended for LVEF ≤35%, atrial fibrillation, LV thrombus, systemic embolism, or bromocriptine use. Bromocriptine suppresses prolactin secretion and has shown encouraging recovery signals in pilot and randomized studies, particularly when added to guideline-directed heart-failure therapy and anticoagulation [27,28]. Its use requires discussion of lactation suppression, thrombotic risk, and local expertise. Severe PPCM may require inotropes, vasodilators, noninvasive or invasive ventilation, temporary mechanical circulatory support, durable LV assist device therapy, or transplantation [25,26].

Prognosis is variable. Many women improve substantially within 3–6 months, but recovery may continue for years; others progress to chronic dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, or death [20-23,29]. Favorable features include LVEF ≥30–35% at diagnosis, smaller LV end-diastolic dimension, early diagnosis, and rapid initiation of therapy. Markedly reduced LVEF, LV dilatation, right ventricular dysfunction, African ancestry in some cohorts, and delayed presentation predict poorer recovery [21-23]. Heart-failure therapy is usually continued for at least 12–24 months after normalization and tapered only cautiously with imaging and biomarker surveillance [29].

Subsequent pregnancy is a major counseling issue. Persistent LV dysfunction is associated with high relapse risk, severe heart failure, and maternal death, and pregnancy is generally discouraged. Even after apparent recovery, relapse can occur; therefore, preconception assessment, shared decision-making, and close monitoring throughout pregnancy and postpartum are essential [30]. Future priorities include validated risk scores, equitable access to cardio-obstetric care, genotype-guided counseling, and trials clarifying bromocriptine, lactation-compatible therapies, and optimal duration of treatment.
